title: Evolution & Genetics · Episode 2
chapters: Island evolution: giants, dwarfs and the dodo
Symbiosis: the partnerships that built life

units.t: Evolution & Genetics. Episode two.
In this episode: Island evolution: giants, dwarfs and the dodo, Symbiosis: the partnerships that built life and The human story.
Part one. Island evolution: giants, dwarfs and the dodo.
Strand animals on an island and strange things happen.
Elephants shrink, rats grow huge and birds forget how to fly.
Natural laboratories.
Islands have taught biologists more about evolution than almost anywhere.
Colonists that drift, fly or blow in are cut off from their relatives, often with few competitors and no large predators, and over generations they can change dramatically.
Darwin's 1835 visit to the Galapagos helped shape his thinking.
Galapagos finches show adaptive radiation, where one ancestor spreads into many forms.
Over about two million years, one colonising group became more than a dozen species, with beaks for crushing seeds, probing cactus flowers, catching insects or even drinking seabird blood.
After a severe drought in 1977 left only large, hard seeds on Daphne Major, Peter and Rosemary Grant found that bigger-beaked birds survived better and the next generation had larger beaks.
Evolution can be measured within years.
The island rule.
Biologists have noticed a broad tendency nicknamed the island rule.
Large mammals stranded on islands often become smaller over generations, perhaps because food is limited and there are fewer predators to outgrow.
Small animals such as rodents often become larger, perhaps because they no longer need to hide from predators and face less competition.
The fossil record is full of examples.
Dwarf elephants, some about the size of a large pig, once lived on Mediterranean islands including Sicily, Malta and Crete.
On the Indonesian island of Flores, there were dwarf relatives of elephants alongside giant rats.
The rule is a tendency rather than a law, and scientists still debate how consistent it is, but the examples are striking.
The hobbit of Flores.
In 2003 researchers excavating Liang Bua cave on Flores found the skeleton of an adult human relative who stood about a metre tall.
It was named Homo floresiensis and quickly nicknamed the hobbit.
Its brain was about the size of a chimpanzee's, yet stone tools were found in the same cave layers.
Later work dated the remains to between roughly 100,000 and 60,000 years ago.
How the hobbits came to be so small is still debated.
One idea is that they descended from Homo erectus and shrank under island conditions, like the island's elephants.
Another is that they came from an older, already small-bodied lineage.
Either way, island life shaped human evolution too.
Forgetting how to fly.
Flying is expensive.
It needs big muscles and a light, demanding body.
On islands without ground predators, many birds evolved to give it up.
The dodo of Mauritius was a large, flightless relative of pigeons, and its closest living relative is the Nicobar pigeon.
New Zealand, with no native land mammals other than bats, became a kingdom of birds, including the giant moa, the kiwi and the kakapo, a heavy, flightless, nocturnal parrot.
Losing flight was sensible until humans arrived with rats, cats, pigs and hunting.
The dodo was gone within a century of Dutch sailors landing in 1598, with the last widely accepted sighting in 1662.
The moa vanished within a few centuries of people reaching New Zealand.
Fragile and precious.
Island species often evolve without defences against newcomers, so they are especially vulnerable.
A large share of recorded animal extinctions in the past five centuries have been island species, many caused by introduced rats, cats and other invaders.
Australia has a famous case.
On Lord Howe Island, a large, flightless stick insect disappeared after black rats came ashore from a shipwreck in 1918.
In 2001, researchers found a tiny surviving population on Ball's Pyramid, a sheer volcanic spire in the ocean nearby.
Captive breeding programs have since raised many more.
In 2019 a major operation began to eradicate rodents from Lord Howe, opening the possibility of returning the insect home.
Islands show both how easily species are lost and how they can be saved.
The key idea: Islands isolate living things, and Galapagos finches show how fast evolution can run there.
Part two. Symbiosis: the partnerships that built life.
Nearly every cell in your body contains descendants of ancient bacteria.
Life on Earth is less a war of all against all than a tangle of deals, partnerships and double-crosses.
Deals, not just wars.
Biologists sort close living-together relationships by who benefits.
In mutualism, both partners gain: bees collect nectar while pollinating flowers.
In commensalism, one gains while the other is barely affected, like barnacles riding on a whale.
In parasitism, one gains at the other's expense.
The German botanist Anton de Bary coined the word symbiosis in 1879.
These boxes are useful, but nature rarely respects them.
A relationship can turn from helpful to harmful as conditions change, and each partner is under pressure to take a little more than it gives.
Symbiosis is best seen as a spectrum of bargains, constantly renegotiated by evolution.
Bacteria inside your cells.
Life's most important partnership began well over a billion years ago.
A single-celled organism took in a bacterium and, instead of digesting it, came to depend on it.
That bacterium became the mitochondrion, which powers our cells using oxygen.
Later, an early cell took in a photosynthetic bacterium, which became the chloroplast in plants and algae.
In the 1960s, the American biologist Lynn Margulis championed this idea, called endosymbiosis, against widespread scepticism.
The evidence now backs her.
Mitochondria and chloroplasts have their own small circular DNA, bacteria-like ribosomes and double membranes, and they divide by splitting in two.
Complex life, including us, is a partnership at its core.
Lichens and corals.
A lichen looks like a single organism, but it is a fungus living with an alga or a cyanobacterium.
The fungus provides structure and shelter, and its partner makes food from sunlight.
Together they colonise bare rock, tree bark and frozen tundra where neither could live alone.
In 2016, researchers found that many lichens also contain a yeast, a third partner that went unnoticed for over a century.
Reef-building corals work similarly.
Their cells house microscopic algae that photosynthesise and pass much of their food to the coral.
When the water becomes too hot, the partnership breaks down.
The coral expels the algae and turns white, an event known as coral bleaching.
Deals and double-crosses.
A fig starts as an enclosed cluster of tiny flowers, and only a fig wasp, usually specialised to one or a few fig species, can pollinate it.
A female squeezes in, often losing her wings, pollinates some flowers, lays eggs in others and dies.
Her offspring mate inside, and the females leave carrying pollen.
Neither partner can reproduce without the other, and the bond is tens of millions of years old.
Partnerships invite cheating.
Bluestreak cleaner wrasse remove parasites from larger fish, but would often rather nibble their protective mucus.
Clients chase cheats away, and cleaners behave better when other fish are watching.
The sabre-toothed blenny goes further: it mimics a cleaner, then bites chunks from fish.
Partners close to home.
In parts of Africa, the greater honeyguide leads people to wild bees' nests, then eats the wax left once humans open the hive.
Yao honey hunters in northern Mozambique summon the bird with a special trilling call, and a 2016 study found it responded to that call far more than to other sounds.
Our microbes matter too.
Trillions of bacteria, mostly in the gut, help digest food, train the immune system and fend off germs.
The claim that they outnumber our cells ten to one is a myth: a 2016 study put the ratio closer to one to one.
Wolbachia bacteria introduced into Aedes aegypti mosquitoes reduce their ability to spread dengue.
The World Mosquito Program, which began in Australia, released them in north Queensland, where local outbreaks have since become very rare.
The key idea: Symbiosis is a spectrum of close partnerships, from mutual benefit to parasitism, renegotiated as conditions change.
Part three. The human story.
For most of the last few hundred thousand years, we weren't alone: several kinds of human shared the planet, and some of them are in your DNA.
Cousins, not descendants.
Humans didn't evolve from chimpanzees.
Both lineages descend from a shared ancestral ape that lived in Africa roughly 6 to 7 million years ago, and both have kept evolving since.
Species on our side of the split are called hominins.
Their family tree is a bushy shrub, not a ladder, with several branches living at once and most ending in extinction.
We are the only surviving twig.
In 1974 in Ethiopia, Donald Johanson's team found about 40 per cent of a skeleton they named Lucy, after the Beatles song playing in camp.
She was an Australopithecus afarensis who lived about 3.
2 million years ago, around a metre tall with a chimp-sized brain, yet her hips and legs show she walked upright.
Footprints at Laetoli, Tanzania, about 3.
6 million years old, confirm it.
Tools, brains and travel.
The oldest known stone tools, from Lomekwi in Kenya, are about 3.
3 million years old, older than our genus, Homo.
From around 2.
5 million years ago, sharp flakes become common across East Africa, and early Homo species such as Homo habilis appear, though exactly which species belong where is debated.
Better tools gave access to meat and marrow, which probably fuelled larger brains.
Homo erectus appeared about 2 million years ago, with long legs and a body much like ours, and made shaped stone hand axes.
It was the first hominin known to leave Africa: fossils about 1.
8 million years old have been found in Georgia, and the species reached China and Java, where it may have survived until around 110,000 years ago.
When hominins learned to control fire is debated.
Sapiens and our relatives.
Our species evolved in Africa.
The oldest fossils generally assigned to it, from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, are about 300,000 years old.
Many researchers think modern humans emerged across Africa, with regional populations exchanging genes, rather than in one small cradle.
When modern humans spread out of Africa, they met other humans.
Neanderthals lived across Europe and western Asia from roughly 400,000 until about 40,000 years ago, and were skilled toolmakers who buried some of their dead.
Denisovans are known mainly from DNA, first read in 2010 from a finger bone in Siberia.
Both interbred with our ancestors.
People with ancestry from outside Africa typically carry 1 to 2 per cent Neanderthal DNA, and many Papua New Guineans and Aboriginal Australians carry several per cent Denisovan DNA.
Out of Africa to Australia.
The main dispersal of modern humans out of Africa happened roughly 60,000 to 70,000 years ago.
People moved along coasts and across Asia with remarkable speed, and reaching Australia required sea crossings even when sea levels were low.
Excavations at Madjedbebe rock shelter in Arnhem Land have produced dates of about 65,000 years, though some researchers argue for closer to 50,000; the range is still debated.
At Lake Mungo in New South Wales, the burials of Mungo Lady and Mungo Man are around 40,000 years old.
Many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples also hold that they have always been on this land.
What it means for us.
The human story has a few big lessons.
First, all living people belong to one young species, and genetically we are very similar; there is more genetic variation within Africa than between Africa and the rest of the world.
Second, being the only human species is unusual.
For most of hominin history, several kinds of human lived at once.
Third, the story keeps changing as new fossils and ancient DNA emerge, so treat any date as a best current estimate.
When you read a headline about a 'missing link', remember the family tree is a bush, not a chain.
Other species, like the small Homo floresiensis of Indonesia, also survived until relatively recently.
The key idea: Humans didn't descend from chimpanzees; we share an ancestor from 6 to 7 million years ago, and upright walking came long before big brains.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What did Peter and Rosemary Grant observe after the 1977 drought on Daphne Major?
Answer. The next generation had larger beaks.
Question two. What is commensalism?
Answer. One gains, the other is barely affected.
Question three. What did Lucy's skeleton show about human evolution?
Answer. Walking upright came long before big brains.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
